analysis.one_liner: Weakens endangered species protections and pays landowners for habitat restrictions.
analysis.headline: A bill by seven Republican senators to loosen Endangered Species Act rules died in committee without ever getting a Senate vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Sponsored by Sen. Steve Symms of Idaho and six other Republican senators, the bill would rewrite the Endangered Species Act to make it much harder to list a species as endangered, replace costly recovery plans with weaker "stabilization" plans that expire unless Congress votes to keep the species listed, and compensate landowners through tax credits and property-rights protections. It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in August 1992 and never received a hearing or vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Timber companies, real estate developers, mining and agricultural interests, and other Western land users would gain the most: the bill raises the scientific bar for listing species, requires detailed economic analysis before protections take effect, exempts the Northern Spotted Owl and all subspecies and distinct populations from protection, and automatically strips protection from any species whose recovery plan costs over $10 million unless Congress extends it. Owners of land designated as critical habitat would get a federal tax credit worth 110 percent of their state and local property taxes, plus a deduction for habitat expenses, and a legal defense against enforcement after three years of habitat management.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Developers, timber firms, and large landowners

how_it_helps.text: Narrows the definition of protected 'species' to exclude subspecies and distinct populations, and singles out the Northern Spotted Owl — the species at the center of Pacific Northwest logging disputes — by name for exclusion from protection.

Raises the standard for listing so a species counts as endangered only if destruction is 'imminent' and the evidence meets 'adequate and verifiable scientifically valid data' standards, and lets courts review listing decisions at the request of affected parties — making protections slower and easier to challenge.

Requires recovery plans to document costs, projected economic impacts by sector, and private property to be compensated, and any species whose recovery would cost more than $10 million would be demoted to a weaker 'stabilization plan' and lose its listing automatically unless Congress passes a law to extend it.

Pays landowners: a federal income tax credit of 110 percent of state and local taxes on property designated as critical habitat, a deduction for habitat expenses, a 90-day notice requirement before habitat designation, and a defense against 'harm or harass' charges for owners who manage non-critical habitat for three years.

Shields water rights from being affected by species protections without compensation and bars the Act from altering interstate water allocations — a provision of direct value to Western irrigation and agricultural water users.

analysis.who_pays: The public pays twice: federal revenue lost to the 110 percent tax credits and deductions would be made up by other taxpayers, and weakened listing, recovery, and enforcement rules would shift the cost of development and resource extraction onto wildlife and the ecosystems ordinary people depend on. Taxpayers would also fund the new Biodiversity Foundation's grants, whose projects would be exempt from environmental review.

drawbacks.text: The automatic delisting trigger — any species with a recovery plan costing over $10 million loses protection unless Congress affirmatively votes to extend it — could abandon exactly the species whose survival requires the most effort, since recovery for large-habitat species routinely exceeds that figure.

The bill's own tax credits and property compensation would be a direct cost to federal revenue: a 110 percent credit of state and local taxes on critical-habitat land plus a new deduction against adjusted gross income would be paid for by all taxpayers.

Requiring 'adequate and verifiable' data and 'imminent' destruction would block listings based on the best available evidence — the standard the current Act uses, because complete population data rarely exists for rare species — meaning some species could slide toward extinction before legally qualifying for help.

Conservation projects funded through the new Biodiversity Foundation would be deemed automatically compliant with the Endangered Species Act and exempt from the National Environmental Policy Act's review requirements, removing public environmental scrutiny of those projects.

Redefining 'take' to require knowledge or deliberate ignorance, and barring scientists who petitioned for a listing from helping write the recovery plan, would make enforcement harder and remove the experts most familiar with a species from planning its recovery.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill contains a few genuine incentives — voluntary conservation easements on private land, grants to states, and compensation for landowners — but they are bundled with a wholesale weakening of the Act's core machinery: a higher listing bar, economic analysis at every step, automatic expiration of protections for expensive species, and named exemptions like the Northern Spotted Owl. An honest supporter would have to concede that the incentives are small next to the delisting trigger, which could strand the very species that need the most help, and that the compensation and tax credits transfer public money to private landowners while reducing the protections the public receives in exchange.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced in August 1992 and sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. Steve Symms of Idaho introduced the bill on August 10, 1992, joined by six Republican cosponsors — Craig, Garn, Hatch, Lott, Thurmond, and Helms.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, which took no further action on it.
No vote ever occurred in either chamber; the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Endangered species kept the protections they had under the existing law, and the public avoided paying the bill's new tax credits and compensation scheme. The property-rights, timber, and development interests the seven sponsors wrote it for got nothing.

for.name: Sen. Steven D. Symms
for.role: U.S. Senator from Idaho; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Progressive Endangered Species Act of 1992 and wrote its core provisions raising listing standards, adding property compensation, and exempting the Northern Spotted Owl.

for.name: 6 Senate Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors (Sens. Craig of Idaho, Garn of Utah, Hatch of Utah, Lott of Mississippi, Thurmond of South Carolina, Helms of North Carolina)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no further recorded action followed.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on August 10, 1992 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors were Republicans — six from Western or Southern states with large federal land and resource industries — but the bill never reached a vote, so no partisan division was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill excludes subspecies and distinct populations from protection and exempts the Northern Spotted Owl by name — the species whose 1990 listing triggered drastic logging cuts in Pacific Northwest old-growth forests. It would have reopened that habitat to harvest at the public's expense in reduced forest protection.

Higher listing standards, mandatory economic-impact analysis, a 90-day notice before habitat designation, and automatic delisting of species whose recovery costs over $10 million would all loosen the habitat restrictions that can stop or reshape projects.

industries.industry: Agriculture, ranching, and Western water users
industries.note: The bill bars species protections from injuring state-law water rights without just compensation and from altering interstate water allocations, and gives landowners a three-year safe harbor against enforcement — directly easing constraints on irrigation and grazing.

A 110 percent federal tax credit on state and local taxes for critical-habitat property, plus a deduction for habitat expenses, would compensate a subset of landowners at every other taxpayer's expense. It is a genuine private benefit, but one funded by the public.
